newsitem.title: USA: Memphis at odds with Tennessee incorporation law.
newsitem.headline: Memphis at odds with Tennessee incorporation law.

text.p: The Memphis City Council voted to annex two of the three suburbs seeking to incorporate as independent communities, a move aimed at forcing a legal challenge to Tennessee's new incorporation law.

Under the old law, cities could not incorporate within five miles of an existing large municipality or within three miles of an existing small municipality. New towns were required to have at least 1,500 residents.
Under the new law that took effect in April, only 225 residents are needed to form a new communtiy, and new towns can spring up right outside the city limits of existing towns.
The new law also gives incorporation of new towns priority over any annexation attempt by neighboring communities.
The law, which was approved by the General Assembly and signed by Go. Don Sundquist, provides a year-long window of opportunity for neighborhoods seeking to incorporate. It expires April 19, 1998.

Since it took effect, three prosperous Memphis suburbs have filed petitions seeking to incorporate. Government officials believe many more neighborhoods will seek incorporation, which could weaken tax revenue streams in existing municipalities.
The new legislation was championed by Lt. Gov John Wilder, who said he wanted to help a community in his district, Hickory Withe, avoid annexation.
Joe Sweat, a spokesman for Tennessee Municipal League, said the organziation would go to court if necessary to argue that the new law was meant to apply only to Hickory Withe.
